title: Finite scheme-theoretic adjoint kernel of a semisimple algebraic group
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $G$ be a smooth connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Suppose $G$ is semisimple: it has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable closed normal subgroup scheme, where solvable means that the successive commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. Let $\mathfrak g=T_{G/k,e}$ be its tangent space at the identity [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. Write $\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$ for the group scheme whose $R$-points are the invertible $R$-linear maps on $\mathfrak g\otimes_k R$. Let $\operatorname{Ad}_G:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$ be the homomorphism induced by differentiating conjugation. The scheme-theoretic kernel $\ker\operatorname{Ad}_G=G\times_{\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)}\operatorname{Spec}k$, with the second map the identity section, is finite over $k$: it is the spectrum of a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. This includes every characteristic and the trivial group; the kernel need not be smooth or reduced.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 6.3.16, printed p.229, first implication: semisimple geometric fibres give finite geometric kernels of the adjoint representation. Proposition 3.3.8, printed p.102, identifies the reductive adjoint kernel with the scheme centre. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this algebraic-group theorem.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], $G$ is reductive (a semisimple group is reductive) and has a split maximal torus $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$. Put $X=X^*(T)$ and let $\Phi\subset X$ be the roots, i.e. the nonzero $T$-characters occurring in $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. The field $k$ is Noetherian (its only ideals are $(0)$ and $(1)$); [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-noetherian-finite-presentation] applied to the coordinate algebra makes $G$ finitely presented. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-affine-adjoint-kernel-calculus] with $A=k$ and $J=G$. Its module $L=\ker(G(k[\epsilon])\to G(k))$ is the set of $k$-morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}k[\epsilon]\to G$ lying over the identity point, i.e. the tangent space $\mathfrak g=T_{G/k,e}$ of the statement, and in both descriptions a tangent vector is $c+\epsilon d$ with $d$ a derivation at the identity and the linear operations are the pointwise ones on $d$. The homomorphism $\operatorname{Ad}_G:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$ of that node is conjugation on dual-number points, i.e. the differentiated conjugation of the statement, and its scheme-theoretic kernel is $K=\ker\operatorname{Ad}_G=G\times_{\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)}\operatorname{Spec}k$. That node gives that $K$ is a closed normal subgroup scheme of $G$; for a commutative $k$-algebra $R$, $K(R)$ is the set of $g\in G(R)$ acting as the identity on $R\otimes_k\mathfrak g\simeq\operatorname{Lie}(G)(R)$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.8, printed p.102; proof of Proposition 6.3.16, printed p.229. Read online; local archive WANTED.

proof.text: The group $M=X/L$ is a quotient of $X\simeq\mathbf Z^r$, hence finitely generated. Apply [lem-sbc-finitely-generated-abelian-group-structure] to $M$. Since its indexing set is finite, this gives $M\simeq\mathbf Z^{r'}\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^s\mathbf Z/n_i\mathbf Z$, where each $n_i\geq1$ (factors of order one are allowed). The group algebra $k[M]$ of step 2 is the one of [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-group-geometric-criteria] (same basis, multiplication and Hopf operations), so that node identifies $Z(G)\simeq D_k(M)$ as a group scheme with $\mathbf G_m^{r'}\times\prod_i\mu_{n_i}$.

source.place: Corollary 17.62(a),(b), printed p.372; Proposition 12.3 and Remark 12.5, p.232; Theorem 12.9, pp.233--234.

proof.text: In this product, $\mathbf G_m^{r'}\times\{1\}$ is a closed subgroup: in each $\mu_{n_i}$ factor it is cut out by $t_i-1$. Its image $H\subseteq Z(G)\subseteq G$ is central, hence normal in $G$, and commutative, hence solvable. It is a torus, so it is smooth and connected by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus]. The semisimplicity hypothesis on $G$ therefore forces $H=1$. If $r'>0$, the Laurent coordinate $z_1$ in $k[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_{r'}^{\pm1}]$ differs from $1$, so $\mathbf G_m^{r'}$ is not the trivial group scheme. Consequently $r'=0$.

source.place: Corollary 17.62(a),(b), printed p.372; Proposition 12.3 and Remark 12.5, p.232; Theorem 12.9, pp.233--234.

proof.text: With $r'=0$, the decomposition in step 3 shows that $M$ is a finite group: it is a finite direct sum of the finite cyclic groups $\mathbf Z/n_i\mathbf Z$. By the explicit group-algebra description in [lem-sfb-reductive-centre-root-quotient], $k[M]$ has basis $(e_m)_{m\in M}$, a finite basis, so the coordinate algebra of $K\times_GT=Z(G)$ is finite-dimensional over $k$. Now $K$ is a closed normal subgroup scheme of the reductive group $G$ (step 1) and $T$ is a split maximal torus, so [lem-sfb-reductive-normal-subgroup-torus-finiteness] with $N=K$, $S=T$ shows that $K$ has finite-dimensional coordinate algebra. $K$ is affine, being closed in the affine $G$, so the definition [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] says that $K\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is finite. For $G=1$ one has $T=1$, $X=0$, $M=0$, $k[0]=k$ and $K=1$. No step asserted that any $\mu_{n_i}$ or $K$ was reduced or smooth, so the argument applies also when the characteristic divides $n_i$.

split_report.summary: Field-level route (maintainer FIX): K=ker Ad is a closed normal subgroup by the smooth-affine adjoint-kernel calculus; its intersection with a split maximal torus T is the intersection of root kernels, which is Z(G)=D_k(X/ZPhi) by the reductive centre-root-quotient node; semisimplicity kills the torus part of X/ZPhi; finiteness of K∩T gives finiteness of K by the normal-subgroup torus-finiteness node. No new nodes and no statement change.
